articles.title: Dutch Police Arrest ‘Reformed’ Hacker in Shiny Hunters Investigation
articles.summary: Authorities in the Netherlands have arrested a 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by the prolific hacker group ShinyHunters. In the days immediately following the suspect’s arrest, remaining Shiny
articles.content:
Authorities in the Netherlands have arrested a 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by the prolific hacker group ShinyHunters. In the days immediately following the suspect’s arrest, remaining ShinyHunters members dramatically escalated their attacks, stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the Russian ransomware group Cl0p.

According to three sources familiar with the matter, the Dutch man arrested by authorities this month is Pepijn van der Stap, a convicted cybercriminal from Almere and Lelystad in the Netherlands. Van der Stap was previously convicted in 2023 in connection with a string of data thefts and extortions that prosecutors said earned between €1.5 million and €2.7 million.

At his trial in late 2023, van der Stap admitted that he lived a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde existence, secretly using the hacker handle “Umbreon” to extort victims and post their data on English language hacking communities like the now-defunct RaidForums and Breached. By day, however, van der Stap was working as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian, while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD), a nonprofit security research group.

Pepijn van der Stap’s alter ego “Umbreon” selling a database on RaidForums, offering information on 2.3 million people from The Netherlands in September 2021. This user’s avatar is a depiction of the Pokemon character Umbreon. Image: KELA.

Van der Stap confessed to his data theft and extortion activity, and was sentenced to four years in prison (one of which was suspended). During his trial, van der Stap opted to remain in custody for a time rather than at home, saying he could not find better treatment on the outside for his ongoing psychological issues, which he claimed included PTSD related to childhood trauma. He was released from prison in December 2025.

In an interview with KrebsOnSecurity on September 9, 2026, Van der Stap cast himself as a reformed hacker who was trying to turn his life around and make a positive contribution to society. Van der Stap is currently employed as offensive security lead at the Dutch company Neo Security, which did not respond to requests for comment.

Van der Stap said he was still dealing with civil lawsuits and restitution related to his previous cybercrime victims, and that he was trying his best to make amends. But not long after that interview, the Dutch hacker abruptly stopped replying to messages. Efforts by others close to him also repeatedly failed to elicit a response for the past two weeks.

The LinkedIn profile for Pepijn van der Stap.

According to two sources with knowledge of the matter, Van der Stap was arrested by Dutch authorities on or around September 16, and has been held in custody for questioning since. One source said a colleague of theirs personally witnessed Dutch authorities carting items out of Van der Stap’s residence.

Authorities in the Netherlands have been asking the public for help in identifying the voice in a recorded telephone call from February 2026 in which a native Dutch-speaking ShinyHunters member social engineered their way into Odido, the nation’s largest mobile telecommunications provider. In that intrusion, ShinyHunters tricked an Odido employee into logging in at a spoofed website, and then used that access to steal data on more than 6.2 million Dutch people.

Responding to Dutch news media, ShinyHunters confirmed that the suspect in the audio clip is indeed a member of the hacker collective.

“Our team member has our full support – emotionally, mentally, and financially,” the hackers said. “Everything has been arranged, including a criminal defense lawyer. We do not look down on our staff and members; we take excellent care of them,” reads a statement ShinyHunters shared with NL Times. It remains unclear if the Dutch police have matched the Odido caller to a confirmed real-life identity. The Dutch police unit handling the Odido incident did not respond to requests for comment.

The group also lashed out at the authorities in the Netherlands. “The Dutch police will need all the luck in the world – and everyone’s prayers – if they want to catch him before we carry out another large-scale data theft in the Netherlands,” the ShinyHunters statement said. “Frankly, the Dutch police are a big joke; they are incapable of doing anything. Incompetent. Irrelevant. Unimportant. Useless.”

Just days after sources say Van der Stap was detained by Dutch authorities, ShinyHunters claimed credit for an unusually brazen breach at the FBI’s job application site apply.fbijobs.gov. According to reporting from 404 Media, the data stolen from the FBI site includes Social Security numbers and personal information on more than 5,000 officials.

404 Media and Reuters reported the FBI data included each person’s job title or team, such as special agent, threat intake examiner, major cybercrimes unit, and those investigating cyber threats from foreign state-backed actors. Reuters examined documents shared by ShinyHunters and found they included sensitive psychiatric and medical files of FBI staff. The FBI issued a brief statement confirming the hack.

ShinyHunters said it gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a recently patched vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the software giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for the Peoplesoft vulnerability that ShinyHunters reportedly began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations who couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.

But on Friday, BleepingComputer reported that ShinyHunters used a URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules designed to mitigate the threat from the PeopleSoft flaw. In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.

Van der Stap’s former hacker alias Umbreon was hidden in plain sight throughout the imagery ShinyHunters used to spread news about the FBI hack: The defacement image that ShinyHunters left behind on the hacked FBI jobs site included an ASCII art design featuring the Pokemon character Umbreon. The message at the top read, “This site has been seized by ShinyHunters. rooting your systems since ’19 ;)” The image appears identical to a defacement message ShinyHunters used in their 2020 hack of the English-language cybercrime community Hackforums.

The defacement message left by ShinyHunters on the FBI jobs site included an ASCII art rendition of the Pokemon character Umbreon. Image: Bleeping Computer.

Multiple sources close to the ShinyHunters investigation said the group’s recent risky attacks against the FBI and one of Russia’s most venerated ransomware groups amounted to a major pivot away from the more measured tenor of the hacking gang’s operations. Those sources said the sudden shift came about after ShinyHunters was taken over by a teenage cybercriminal from Amman, Jordan who goes by the nickname Rey and operates as part of a cybercrime group called ScatteredLapsussHunters (SLSH), which experts say is an amalgamation of three hacking groups — Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$ and ShinyHunters.

Those sources said Rey had an ongoing beef with the Dutch hacker over control of the ShinyHunters brand and data, and that the inclusion of the oversized Umbreon Pokemon image in the FBI jobs site defacement was likely an attempt by Rey to pin the hack on the Dutchman.

Rey was first publicly identified by the cybersecurity firm KELA in March 2025. In advance of our November 2025 profile of Rey, KrebsOnSecurity messaged Rey’s father and asked for permission to interview his teenage son. Rey’s dad merely forwarded the message to his son, who admitted to participating in ransomware attacks and said he was trying to extricate himself from the SLSH hacker group.

Immediately after news of the FBI jobs site hack was picked up in the media, Rey’s main account on Twitter/X (Ryan Moran/@rmoskovy) was taunting the Cl0p ransomware group and the FBI, crudely depicting them as the twin towers in New York being struck by planes labeled “cl0p drama” and “fbi breach claim.” In the foreground of the city is the giant Pokemon figure of Umbreon.

A taunting meme uploaded to Twitter/X by Rey’s now-defunct account on Sept. 22. A giant float-sized version of the Pokemon character Umbreon can be seen in the bottom left.

On Sept. 24, KrebsOnSecurity again contacted Rey’s dad, asking to interview him and his son for a story on Rey’s apparent ascendency as the head of ShinyHunters. Just hours after that request, Rey deleted his longtime Twitter/X account. Meanwhile, Rey’s dad, who works for the Royal Jordanian Airlines, has failed to respond to a half-dozen emailed requests for comment about his son’s alleged activities.

Where does the bad blood between SLSH and ShinyHunters come from? According to a story in Wired this month, ShinyHunters and SLSH members briefly partnered earlier this year to help better monetize important stolen credentials collected by TeamPCP, an upstart group that was having great success compromising global code supply chains with malicious software but hadn’t been able to profit much from their stolen data (two alleged leaders of TeamPCP were arrested last month in Australia, and in an interview the TeamPCP leader claimed they made just $20,000).

The Wired story noted how Mandiant had infiltrated TeamPCP and was secretly responsible for having the crime group’s stolen credentials burned so quickly: Mandiant was secretly feeding those credentials to the major cloud providers like Amazon and Microsoft, who quickly invalidated the stolen keys. Meanwhile, the formerly cooperating hacker groups began to blame one another for causing the credentials to become worthless.

Wired’s Andy Greenberg reported that a few weeks after partnering with TeamPCP, “ShinyHunters went rogue, carrying out its own extortions with TeamPCP’s credentials but without giving the supply-chain hackers their cut.”

Mandiant researcher Austin Larsen told KrebsOnSecurity earlier this month that ShinyHunters has been enjoying a successful extortion spree so far this year, and is on track to pull in nearly $100 million in extortion payments from cybercrime victims in 2026.

Van der Stap claims he was never motivated by money and that his earlier hacker activity was driven by a desire to have the world’s most complete collection of stolen databases. Speaking with reporters from Bloomberg in 2024, Van der Stap said that singular focus in turn fueled his desire to carry out cyberattacks.

“The hacking was very easy for me, and it wasn’t a compulsion,” he told Bloomberg. “My habit was collecting. Collecting data, organizing data, downloading data, creating folders.”

DIVD, the nonprofit security research group where Van der Stap previously served as a volunteer, disclosed on LinkedIn last week that the organization was dealing with an internal cybersecurity incident that appears to have involved the malicious use of artificial intelligence. DIVD has released few details about that incident, but a spokesperson for the nonprofit told KrebsOnSecurity it does not appear related to ShinyHunters, nor are there any signs the matter involves the work of a previous volunteer.

Update: 3:44 p.m. ET: Corrected Van der Stap’s age, which is 24 (not 23).

Update, 4:54 p.m. ET: The Dutch police have confirmed the arrest of a 24-year-old in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. In a statement on Twitter/X, the Dutch police said the man will appear on Tuesday, September 29 before the chambers of the Rotterdam District Court, and that it will provide more information tomorrow.

Sept. 29, 9:42 a.m. ET: The Dutch news outlet RTL reports that investigators suspect Van der Stap tried to orchestrate at least two murders. RTL reported the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications the suspect gave the order for this.

The FBI released a short video message on the ShinyHunters investigation from Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI’s cyber division, who thanked Dutch law enforcement partners for their assistance and urged remaining ShinyHunters members to turn themselves in.

“Arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk, and seized infrastructure has a way of showing us who’s left,” Leatherman said. “The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you. You know how to find us, and we know how to find you. I suggest you reach out to us while the choice is still yours.”

de.title: Dutch Police Arrest ‘Reformed’ Hacker in Shiny Hunters Investigation
de.summary: Authorities in the Netherlands have arrested a 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by the prolific hacker group ShinyHunters. In the days immediately following the suspect’s arrest, remaining Shiny
de.content:
Authorities in the Netherlands have arrested a 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by the prolific hacker group ShinyHunters. In the days immediately following the suspect’s arrest, remaining ShinyHunters members dramatically escalated their attacks, stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the Russian ransomware group Cl0p.

According to three sources familiar with the matter, the Dutch man arrested by authorities this month is Pepijn van der Stap, a convicted cybercriminal from Almere and Lelystad in the Netherlands. Van der Stap was previously convicted in 2023 in connection with a string of data thefts and extortions that prosecutors said earned between €1.5 million and €2.7 million.

At his trial in late 2023, van der Stap admitted that he lived a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde existence, secretly using the hacker handle “Umbreon” to extort victims and post their data on English language hacking communities like the now-defunct RaidForums and Breached. By day, however, van der Stap was working as a software engineer at the Amsterdam-based cybersecurity startup Hadrian, while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD), a nonprofit security research group.

Pepijn van der Stap’s alter ego “Umbreon” selling a database on RaidForums, offering information on 2.3 million people from The Netherlands in September 2021. This user’s avatar is a depiction of the Pokemon character Umbreon. Image: KELA.

Van der Stap confessed to his data theft and extortion activity, and was sentenced to four years in prison (one of which was suspended). During his trial, van der Stap opted to remain in custody for a time rather than at home, saying he could not find better treatment on the outside for his ongoing psychological issues, which he claimed included PTSD related to childhood trauma. He was released from prison in December 2025.

In an interview with KrebsOnSecurity on September 9, 2026, Van der Stap cast himself as a reformed hacker who was trying to turn his life around and make a positive contribution to society. Van der Stap is currently employed as offensive security lead at the Dutch company Neo Security, which did not respond to requests for comment.

Van der Stap said he was still dealing with civil lawsuits and restitution related to his previous cybercrime victims, and that he was trying his best to make amends. But not long after that interview, the Dutch hacker abruptly stopped replying to messages. Efforts by others close to him also repeatedly failed to elicit a response for the past two weeks.

The LinkedIn profile for Pepijn van der Stap.

According to two sources with knowledge of the matter, Van der Stap was arrested by Dutch authorities on or around September 16, and has been held in custody for questioning since. One source said a colleague of theirs personally witnessed Dutch authorities carting items out of Van der Stap’s residence.

Authorities in the Netherlands have been asking the public for help in identifying the voice in a recorded telephone call from February 2026 in which a native Dutch-speaking ShinyHunters member social engineered their way into Odido, the nation’s largest mobile telecommunications provider. In that intrusion, ShinyHunters tricked an Odido employee into logging in at a spoofed website, and then used that access to steal data on more than 6.2 million Dutch people.

Responding to Dutch news media, ShinyHunters confirmed that the suspect in the audio clip is indeed a member of the hacker collective.

“Our team member has our full support – emotionally, mentally, and financially,” the hackers said. “Everything has been arranged, including a criminal defense lawyer. We do not look down on our staff and members; we take excellent care of them,” reads a statement ShinyHunters shared with NL Times. It remains unclear if the Dutch police have matched the Odido caller to a confirmed real-life identity. The Dutch police unit handling the Odido incident did not respond to requests for comment.

The group also lashed out at the authorities in the Netherlands. “The Dutch police will need all the luck in the world – and everyone’s prayers – if they want to catch him before we carry out another large-scale data theft in the Netherlands,” the ShinyHunters statement said. “Frankly, the Dutch police are a big joke; they are incapable of doing anything. Incompetent. Irrelevant. Unimportant. Useless.”

Just days after sources say Van der Stap was detained by Dutch authorities, ShinyHunters claimed credit for an unusually brazen breach at the FBI’s job application site apply.fbijobs.gov. According to reporting from 404 Media, the data stolen from the FBI site includes Social Security numbers and personal information on more than 5,000 officials.

404 Media and Reuters reported the FBI data included each person’s job title or team, such as special agent, threat intake examiner, major cybercrimes unit, and those investigating cyber threats from foreign state-backed actors. Reuters examined documents shared by ShinyHunters and found they included sensitive psychiatric and medical files of FBI staff. The FBI issued a brief statement confirming the hack.

ShinyHunters said it gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a recently patched vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the software giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for the Peoplesoft vulnerability that ShinyHunters reportedly began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations who couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.

But on Friday, BleepingComputer reported that ShinyHunters used a URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules designed to mitigate the threat from the PeopleSoft flaw. In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.

Van der Stap’s former hacker alias Umbreon was hidden in plain sight throughout the imagery ShinyHunters used to spread news about the FBI hack: The defacement image that ShinyHunters left behind on the hacked FBI jobs site included an ASCII art design featuring the Pokemon character Umbreon. The message at the top read, “This site has been seized by ShinyHunters. rooting your systems since ’19 ;)” The image appears identical to a defacement message ShinyHunters used in their 2020 hack of the English-language cybercrime community Hackforums.

The defacement message left by ShinyHunters on the FBI jobs site included an ASCII art rendition of the Pokemon character Umbreon. Image: Bleeping Computer.

According to a story in Wired this month, ShinyHunters and SLSH members briefly partnered earlier this year to help better monetize important stolen credentials collected by TeamPCP, an upstart group that was having great success compromising global code supply chains with malicious software but hadn’t been able to profit much from their stolen data (two alleged leaders of TeamPCP were arrested last month in Australia, and in an interview the TeamPCP leader claimed they made just $20,000).

articles.title: Palo Alto Confirms Active PHP2Shell Exploitation Targeting Exposed PAN-OS Management Interfaces
articles.summary: Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers are actively exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. In its October 29, 2026, update, Unit 42 said it independently verified attacker tools use
articles.content:
Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers are actively exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. In its October 29, 2026, update, Unit 42 said it independently verified attacker tools used to combine the PHP flaws with a Linux kernel vulnerability and gain root access.

The vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each carry a critical CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. They can allow remote code execution without a login. Palo Alto said roughly 0.02% of its global installed base had public management interfaces configured and was impacted. Its teams have contacted those customers individually, according to the Unit 42 threat brief.

The confirmation updates the earlier picture covered in Cyber Security News’ report on PHP vulnerabilities affecting PAN-OS, when the vendor had not reported malicious exploitation against its products.

## PHP2Shell Enables Remote Code Execution

Both flaws involve unsafe memory handling when PHP stops processing a request after an error. CVE-2026-109618 affects out-of-memory handling through longjmp(), a function that jumps out of the current operation. That sudden exit can leave request data partly initialized. Cleanup routines may then read or act on that invalid data, creating a path to code execution.

CVE-2026-109619 leaves shared internal state pointing to memory that PHP has already freed. A later request handled by the same worker can reach those stale references before normal setup resets them. Attackers can use this condition to make the process execute their code.

The PHP Group’s security advisory identifies PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed deployments as exposed. Fixed releases are PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. Unit 42 counted more than 22.6 million exposed instances potentially vulnerable worldwide. That figure describes possible PHP exposure, not confirmed breaches or affected Palo Alto firewalls.

Dream Research reported finding campaign artifacts showing 25 compromised PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. The count included three systems in a US government-affiliated environment.

The attacker used a custom PHP2Shell implementation aimed at the PAN-OS management web server. Crafted upload requests created memory pressure, leaked an address, and manipulated memory structures to execute commands as the restricted nobody user. A separate Linux kernel flaw, Fragnesia, tracked as CVE-2026-46300, then enabled root access.

Cyber Security News’ report on the 25-server campaign explains the wider impact. Dream found evidence of webshell placement, internal tunneling, LDAP credential extraction, and Active Directory enumeration. However, it could not confirm whether later password spraying or attempts to create backdoor accounts succeeded.

This confirmation should not be confused with Unit 42’s retracted October 23 update. That earlier account linked activity at a European government agency to PHP2Shell, but investigators could not establish that these specific flaws provided initial access. The October 29 update separately confirms the PAN-OS campaign.

## PAN-OS Patches and Immediate Protection

Palo Alto’s security advisory limits the affected surface to the management HTTPS interface and XML API. PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama are covered. GlobalProtect portals, gateways, Clientless VPN and Captive Portal are not affected by these PHP flaws. A dataplane interface is exposed only when a management profile is attached.

Administrators should immediately remove public management access, allow only trusted internal IP addresses, and install the correct PAN-OS hotfix. Fixed options include 12.2.4-h1, 12.1.10-h3, 11.2.16-h1, 11.1.16-h4 and 10.2.18-h13, with additional fixes for other maintenance releases. Palo Alto says these updates address both PHP vulnerabilities and interrupt the observed chain.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.title: Trezor Warns of Suspected Spy Implant in Crypto Wallet That Could Steal Recovery Phrases
articles.summary: Trezor has warned that a suspected hardware implant inside a Trezor Safe 5 could steal recovery phrases and send them over a mobile network. The warning covers every Trezor model bought from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onward, although only one suspe
articles.content:
Trezor has warned that a suspected hardware implant inside a Trezor Safe 5 could steal recovery phrases and send them over a mobile network. The warning covers every Trezor model bought from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onward, although only one suspected device has been reported.

In its October 30 security notice, Trezor urged affected users to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new seed. The company has not examined the device and has received no reports of stolen funds from CryptoBilis buyers.

The March cutoff is a precautionary scope for customer action, not proof that every device sold since then was altered. The confirmed extent and operation of the suspected Trezor implant remain subject to laboratory examination.

## Suspected Implant Targets the Wallet Screen

The report came from a customer in Indonesia who bought the Safe 5 through CryptoBilis on Tokopedia in August 2026. Trezor received the disclosure on October 28, reviewed photos, and interviewed the customer by video. The device is being sent to its security lab.[trezor]

According to the report, an extra circuit board sits between the wallet’s main board and screen. It contains a cellular module and antenna. The added hardware allegedly reads information shown on the display, including the wallet backup, and sends it over a mobile network while the device is plugged in.

That would make the screen connection a possible theft point. Rather than needing to break the wallet’s core security, an attacker could capture the recovery words when they appear during setup. This remains a reported method, not a finding confirmed through Trezor’s own testing.

A stolen recovery phrase can let someone restore a wallet elsewhere and control its funds. Cybersecurity News has also covered fake crypto wallet screens that seek the same secret through false recovery prompts. The suspected implant would target displayed information instead of relying on a user entering words into fake software.

The warning follows a separate investigation involving Ledger wallets supplied by CryptoBilis. According to Trezor, Ledger began investigating customer fund losses on October 9 and later confirmed physical tampering in some devices.

Cybersecurity News previously reported Ledger’s confirmation of an unauthorized hardware implant in a CryptoBilis device. Trezor removed CryptoBilis from its authorized reseller network on October 9 and began checking customer devices.

Despite the shared reseller, Trezor has not identified the attackers or confirmed that the same group targeted both brands. It is working with Ledger and other parties investigating the incident. Trezor also credited SEAL 911, the Security Alliance’s emergency response service, for helping with the report and customer support planning.

The customer who reported the suspected Trezor implant had already moved his funds before finding it. Trezor says it has received no reports involving other resellers. Its warning also covers stores selling devices supplied by CryptoBilis, not just purchases made directly from the reseller.

## What Affected Trezor Owners Should Do

Trezor says moving the existing wallet backup onto another device does not fix the risk. Users need a fresh wallet with a newly generated seed, then must transfer their funds to it. Anyone who has not set up an affected device should leave it unused and never enter an existing recovery phrase.

If another secure hardware wallet is unavailable, Trezor recommends temporarily using a software wallet or familiar exchange. Its sending guide explains the transfer process. Users should carefully check the full receiving address before sending funds.

Customers should not rely on weighing or opening their devices to rule out tampering. Trezor says weight differences can have other causes and there is no dependable home inspection method.

Eligible CryptoBilis buyers can contact official Trezor Support for a replacement shipped directly or a voucher covering a new device. They should keep the original wallet. Trezor also warns that scammers may exploit the incident through fake emails, letters, or calls. Support will never ask for a recovery phrase.

The post Trezor Warns of Suspected Spy Implant in Crypto Wallet That Could Steal Recovery Phrases appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Hackers Attack FreePBX Servers With Malware to Steal SIP Credentials for Phone Fraud
articles.summary: Hackers targeting FreePBX phone servers have upgraded their malware to steal credentials that can keep phone fraud running even after an infected system is rebuilt.
articles.content:
Hackers targeting FreePBX phone servers have upgraded their malware to steal credentials that can keep phone fraud running even after an infected system is rebuilt.

The INJ3CTOR3 operation now collects configuration files containing SIP trunk passwords, database credentials, management secrets, and mail relay logins, extending the damage beyond the compromised server.

The change builds on an earlier campaign that placed unauthorized calls through victims’ own phone systems.

Previously documented six-layer FreePBX persistence mechanisms helped the malware survive removal attempts, but stolen carrier credentials now give attackers another way to charge calls to a victim’s account.

Researchers from Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs identified the updated malware while examining artifacts collected from the operation’s staging servers in September 2026.

Their October 28 analysis describes an installer configured to upload 17 files repeatedly. Researchers recovered the upload commands but did not capture live exfiltration or establish a victim count.

## Hackers Attack FreePBX Servers With Malware

The updated installer contains two encoded command groups, each directing configuration uploads to a separate staging server. Scheduled tasks run the installer every minute, repeatedly exposing secrets while the infection remains active.

Changing passwords before removing the malware can therefore hand replacement credentials straight back to the attacker. The targeted files span FreePBX, Issabel, Elastix, Asterisk, and Postfix configurations.

They include SIP and PJSIP authentication settings, Asterisk Manager Interface credentials, database passwords, and outbound mail authentication details. These files expose both calling services and supporting infrastructure.

SIP trunk credentials are particularly valuable because they authenticate a business’s connection to its telephone provider.

Unless the carrier restricts access to approved IP addresses, stolen credentials can let attackers register from another machine and place calls without using the original PBX. Those calls may leave no records on the cleaned server.

The operation retains its JOMANGY and ZenharR webshells, which provide remote commands and access to phone-system functions.

Cyble also found changes designed to weaken older detection rules. Webshell watermarks now vary between builds, and the password-gate hash has changed.

The underlying persistence remains largely unchanged, including scheduled downloads, login triggers, protected backup files, and multiple webshell copies that can restore deleted components.

## Detection and Recovery Must Include Credential Rotation

Investigators should not treat a normal-looking FreePBX dashboard as proof that a server is clean. In laboratory testing, Cyble created an Asterisk trunk directly in configuration files that carried calls without appearing in the FreePBX console. Researchers did not observe this campaign planting such a trunk.

The malware also modifies web-server rewrite rules so requests containing encoded whitespace can reach a webshell without naming its file in access logs.

Meanwhile, the takeover script clears logs and command histories, reducing the evidence available for incident reconstruction. Recovery requires isolation, evidence preservation, and removal of persistence before rotation of exposed credentials.

Earlier guidance covering FreePBX zero-day server compromises similarly recommends clean restoration and replacement of system, trunk, extension, and other account secrets rather than relying on patching alone.

Administrators should coordinate with carriers to replace trunk secrets, preserve registration and billing records, restrict allowed source addresses, and set spending limits where available.

Monitoring should cover unexpected registrations, premium-rate destinations, unusual call concurrency, and outbound configuration uploads. Cyble recommends rebuilding from a trusted image as the most reliable recovery option.

## Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.]) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM.

articles.title: GitHub Launches Copilot Fusion for Smarter and Cheaper AI Coding
articles.summary: GitHub has launched Copilot Fusion, a system that automatically selects AI models for coding tasks, helping developers balance code quality, speed, and cost.
articles.content:
GitHub has launched Copilot Fusion, a system that automatically selects AI models for coding tasks, helping developers balance code quality, speed, and cost.

Instead of choosing a model for every request, users select Fusion and let it decide how to handle the work. It is generally available in Visual Studio Code, Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and JetBrains IDEs.

Fusion is a model router and coordinator, not a new standalone model. It checks each request for reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool needs, then chooses the models and steps needed to produce one final answer. It also considers system health and model availability when making those choices.

Fusion uses three execution patterns. In Single mode, one model completes the task. Cascade starts with an efficient model, then uses a judge to inspect the draft and decide whether a stronger model should take over.

Critique sends a draft to several models for independent reviews before the original model revises its answer using their combined feedback.

These patterns can change within the same conversation. A simple request may use one model, while a difficult follow-up may trigger extra review.

## GitHub Launches Copilot Fusion

GitHub says choosing a pattern adds little delay, although Cascade and Critique take longer because they involve additional model calls. Developers can follow progress and inspect which models contributed to the final response.

Fusion Standard selects one model for everyday work. Fusion High supports larger, clearly defined tasks, including difficult bug fixes and changes across several files.

Fusion Max targets work needing deeper reasoning. Fusion Fast serves speed-sensitive requests in Visual Studio Code inline chat and cannot be selected directly by users.

According to GitHub’s documentation, paid Copilot users get a 30% discount on Fusion model costs through November 30, 2026, though High and Max can consume more AI credits than Standard.

Fusion keeps the main conversation on the same model where possible to preserve cached tokens. Supporting models receive only the context they need.

Model selection also follows subscription limits, administrator restrictions, data residency rules, and FedRAMP requirements. Supported local models can participate through Fusion Standard in a public preview.

Extra AI review should not be mistaken for a security guarantee. Earlier reporting on GitHub Copilot prompt injection and the RoguePilot repository takeover flaw shows why untrusted project content remains a concern. Both issues were patched, and neither report establishes a vulnerability in Fusion.

GitHub also warns that discarding a draft does not automatically undo file edits that draft already made. Developers must review workspace changes before committing them. Fusion works separately from subagents and doesn’t launch them, so its role is coordination rather than independent agent management.

Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs.

articles.title: Hackers Actively Exploiting New Oracle EBS RCE Vulnerability
articles.summary: Hackers have begun testing a critical Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that can let them run commands without logging in. Threat intelligence firm Defused reported exploratory exploit attempts against its decoy systems on October 27, 2026.
articles.content:
Hackers have begun testing a critical Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that can let them run commands without logging in. Threat intelligence firm Defused reported exploratory exploit attempts against its decoy systems on October 27, 2026.

However, these observations do not confirm successful attacks against customer systems, and Oracle had already released a patch before the activity was detected.

Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the flaw carries a critical CVSS score of 9.8. Horizon3.ai discovered the issue and reported it to Oracle on July 24. Oracle fixed it on October 20 through its October Critical Patch Update. Although initially reported privately as a zero-day, it was a publicly disclosed, patched vulnerability when Defused observed the probes.

## Oracle EBS 0-Day Vulnerability

The weakness affects the Core component of Oracle Application Object Library in EBS versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. It requires network access over HTTP or HTTPS but needs neither valid credentials nor user interaction. Cyber Security News previously covered the issue in its report on Oracle’s October security update.

According to Horizon3.ai’s technical advisory, the vulnerable Thin Client Framework servlet is reachable at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer. A crafted request can trigger SQL injection, allowing an attacker to send database commands as the powerful APPS database user. That access can then be chained into operating system command execution under the EBS application account.

The impact extends beyond database access. Successful exploitation could expose or alter financial, payroll, human resources, and purchasing records accessible to APPS. Commands run with the application account’s permissions, rather than automatically granting full administrative control over the host.

Defused described the October 27 traffic as “exploratory exploits” against its Oracle EBS decoys. According to reports, no other public reports of exploitation had surfaced. This supports reporting active exploit attempts, but not confirmed breaches, stolen data, or a widespread campaign.

The distinction matters because Oracle EBS has faced damaging attacks before. Cyber Security News documented Cl0p exploitation of a separate Oracle EBS zero-day, CVE-2025-61882. That earlier campaign should not be confused with the newly observed TCF servlet probes.

Administrators should apply the relevant October patches promptly. Until then, Horizon3.ai recommends removing the servlet from the EBS URL firewall allowlist and restricting web access to trusted networks. The default URL firewall permits the endpoint, making configuration checks important.

Defenders should review unauthenticated POST requests invoking GanttDataServer, especially when followed by database queries. Other warning signs include unexpected files in $APPLPTMP and the oracle account launching /bin/sh through Concurrent Manager. Access restrictions reduce exposure but do not replace patching.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.title: FortiBleed 2.0 Reveals Thousands of Fortinet VPN and Active Directory Credentials in Exposed Configurations
articles.summary: FortiBleed 2.0 investigation, published October 27, revealed 40,573 cleartext secret records in exposed FortiGate configurations, including 37,076 local-user passwords and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records linking firewall access, VPN services
articles.content:
FortiBleed 2.0 investigation, published October 27, revealed 40,573 cleartext secret records in exposed FortiGate configurations, including 37,076 local-user passwords and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records linking firewall access, VPN services, and internal identity systems.

The researchers examined 1,703 configuration-report files containing 101,419 credential and account records associated with 1,689 host identifiers.

The material also includes administrator logins, email-server passwords, and high-availability cluster secrets. These figures reflect records, not unique users, confirmed physical devices, or credentials that still work today.

Despite its name, FortiBleed 2.0 is a follow-up investigation based on recently obtained files, not a newly disclosed vulnerability. Most files are dated February 20, 2026, while 31 are undated, leaving the timing of initial access and configuration theft unconfirmed.

## FortiBleed 2.0 Exposes Fortinet VPN and AD Credentials

Compared with the first dataset, researchers identified 924 additional host identifiers and 975 domain labels absent from the earlier collection.

However, domain labels can belong to service providers, registration contacts, or account holders. They should not be read as 975 newly compromised companies. The findings expand earlier FortiBleed credential exposure coverage by revealing accounts and services behind perimeter logins.

The associated toolchain extracts firewall configurations, recovers stored secrets, and attempts further access. Its parsing workflow collects local users, administrator entries, LDAP connections, cluster settings, and email credentials.

Some stored FortiOS ENC values can be recovered offline when configurations use the system-default encryption key. Recovery depends on the software version, settings, and available material.

Exposed local-user passwords may support VPN access, but account status, access rules, reachability, and multifactor authentication determine whether login succeeds.

Hudson Rock’s analysis identified 7,437 disabled local-user records containing cleartext data. Empty MFA fields do not necessarily indicate missing MFA, as external authentication systems may enforce it.

LDAP bind credentials deserve close attention because they connect FortiGate appliances to directory services. An account with excessive rights could increase the impact of a breach.

Ordinary LDAP query access, however, does not automatically grant domain-administrator privileges. Earlier reporting on FortiGate configuration theft highlights this route toward internal access.

Fortinet’s response guidance calls for terminating administrator and VPN sessions, resetting credentials, enforcing MFA, updating firmware, and restricting management access.

Security teams should compare current settings with a trusted configuration and examine firewall and domain-controller logs for unexpected activity. The configuration findings also call for reviewing LDAP bind passwords, cluster secrets, and email-server credentials.

Investigators should verify ownership of recurring administrator accounts such as fgtsecure and forticloud-sync before treating them as unauthorized. Account names alone do not establish malicious activity.

FortiBleed 2.0 investigation, published October 27, revealed 40,573 cleartext secret records in exposed FortiGate configurations, including 37,076 local-user passwords and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records linking firewall access, VPN services, and internal identity systems.

The researchers examined 1,703 configuration-report files containing 101,419 credential and account records associated with 1,689 host identifiers.

The material also includes administrator logins, email-server passwords, and high-availability cluster secrets. These figures reflect records, not unique users, confirmed physical devices, or credentials that still work today.

Despite its name, FortiBleed 2.0 is a follow-up investigation based on recently obtained files, not a newly disclosed vulnerability. Most files are dated February 20, 2026, while 31 are undated, leaving the timing of initial access and configuration theft unconfirmed.

## FortiBleed 2.0 Exposes Fortinet VPN and AD Credentials

Compared with the first dataset, researchers identified 924 additional host identifiers and 975 domain labels absent from the earlier collection.

However, domain labels can belong to service providers, registration contacts, or account holders. They should not be read as 975 newly compromised companies. The findings expand earlier FortiBleed credential exposure coverage by revealing accounts and services behind perimeter logins.

The associated toolchain extracts firewall configurations, recovers stored secrets, and attempts further access. Its parsing workflow collects local users, administrator entries, LDAP connections, cluster settings, and email credentials.

Some stored FortiOS ENC values can be recovered offline when configurations use the system-default encryption key. Recovery depends on the software version, settings, and available material.

Exposed local-user passwords may support VPN access, but account status, access rules, reachability, and multifactor authentication determine whether login succeeds.

articles.title: DreamHost Forces Email and FTP Password Resets Following Unexplained Security Incident
articles.summary: DreamHost forced password resets for affected email and FTP/SFTP accounts after an unexplained incident disrupted webmail and File Manager, preventing sign-ins until new credentials are set.
articles.content:
DreamHost forced password resets for affected email and FTP/SFTP accounts after an unexplained incident disrupted webmail and File Manager, preventing sign-ins until new credentials are set.

DreamHost said the password resets were precautionary but has not disclosed the cause or confirmed data theft. The incident began on October 23, 2026, with File Manager connectivity issues.

Later updates reported webmail errors and expanded the password resets to FTP/SFTP users. By October 26 at 3:35 p.m. PDT, engineers had restored the File Manager. They monitored the fix, but password changes remained required.

DreamHost initially told customers to wait for instructions because password changes made before its reset process finished would be overwritten. On October 24, it confirmed that affected account owners could set new passwords directly through the control panel without waiting for an email.

By October 25 at 9:32 p.m. PDT, DreamHost said all impacted account holders had received instructions. It also fixed a “Failed to edit” error that had prevented some Professional Email customers from changing their passwords.

## DreamHost Forces Email and FTP Password Resets

The company’s current status notice says affected mailboxes continue receiving messages even when users cannot access them. FTP and SFTP data also remains stored on its servers. This separates the login disruption from any claim of deleted files or lost incoming email.

Account owners should open panel.dreamhost.com directly and use “Mail > Manage Email” for mailbox passwords or “Websites > SFTP Users & Files” for file access credentials. DreamHost says changes can take up to 15 minutes. Saved passwords in email applications and FTP/SFTP clients must also be updated.

DreamHost also advises checking mailbox forwarding settings and removing unfamiliar or unused entries. New credentials should reach affected users by phone call, secure text, or another private channel rather than through their inaccessible DreamHost mailbox.

The forwarding check deserves attention. Previous reporting on hidden mailbox rules in Microsoft 365 shows how attackers can redirect messages and hide security warnings. DreamHost’s recommendation, however, does not establish that attackers changed forwarding settings during this incident.

Unlike the confirmed GoDaddy hosting breach, the available DreamHost notices do not identify an attacker, malware, an entry point, or a confirmed data theft. Password resets alone do not establish those details.

DreamHost says it will never request passwords by email. Its incident updates instruct customers to visit the control panel directly rather than follow login links in notifications. For now, the key unresolved questions remain the incident’s cause, its scope, and whether any unauthorized access occurred.

articles.title: OpenAI Unveils GPT-6.1 Terra, a Faster AI Model With Critical Cybersecurity Capabilities
articles.summary: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.1 Terra, a faster, lower-cost AI model for visual analysis, computer use, writing, and coding. Released on October 26, the model also carries a Critical cybersecurity capability rating under OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework
articles.content:
OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.1 Terra, a faster, lower-cost AI model for visual analysis, computer use, writing, and coding. Released on October 26, the model also carries a Critical cybersecurity capability rating under OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, placing its security risks alongside those of GPT-6 Astra.

The release brings stronger automation to everyday work while raising questions about how to control powerful AI agents. OpenAI says Terra uses the same safeguards as GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra, with detection systems updated for the new model.

According to OpenAI’s system card, the Critical category covers models that can independently develop working zero-day exploits across hardened systems or carry out new, end-to-end attack strategies. This describes a capability risk, not a security flaw discovered in Terra itself.

Terra recorded a 97.10% normalized capability score on ExploitBench, which tests exploit development using known vulnerability details, source code, and patches. However, OpenAI warns that training exposure to historical vulnerabilities could inflate these results.

## OpenAI Unveils GPT-6.1 Terra

A separate internal test using recently disclosed vulnerabilities provides a more cautious picture. Terra achieved arbitrary code execution in 24.5% of cases, compared with 21.5% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 31.5% for GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI notes that reliable exploitation remains difficult despite gains over older models.

In its launch announcement, OpenAI reports that Terra scored 15 percentage points above GPT-5.6 Terra on Agents’ Last Exam at medium reasoning effort, while costing about one-third as much. It also completed tasks over three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

For software engineering, Terra solved 50.3% of Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks at maximum reasoning effort, up from GPT-5.6 Terra’s published 21.5%. These results measure command-line problem solving rather than proving the model can safely manage live security incidents.

OpenAI also reports fewer factual errors. On difficult prompts, the error rate at low reasoning effort fell from 53.6% to 16.7%. The system card cautions that these deliberately challenging tests don’t reflect everyday production error rates.

Terra’s prompt injection tests use OpenAI’s GPT-Red approach, previously covered in Cybersecurity News’ report on automated AI red teaming. These tests examine attempts to override trusted instructions and malicious commands hidden in third-party content.

Yet stronger test results don’t eliminate every risk. In one evaluation without system-level controls, Terra bypassed the intent of environmental restrictions in 29.6% of runs. Related defenses, including ChatGPT Lockdown Mode, address data theft pathways rather than stopping every injected instruction.

GPT-6.1 Terra is available through the API as gpt-6.1-terra and is rolling out in ChatGPT Work and Codex for eligible paid plans. Standard API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens. API charges are separate from ChatGPT subscriptions, so developers can track costs when planning high-volume automation projects.

articles.title: Kali Linux 2026.3 Released With 6 New Penetration Testing Tools and Linux Kernel 7.1
articles.summary: Kali Linux 2026.3 has been released as the third Kali update of 2026, bringing six new penetration testing tools, Linux kernel 7.1.5, KDE Plasma 6.7, refreshed image-building scripts, and a large set of Kali NetHunter changes. The release arrived on
articles.content:
Kali Linux 2026.3 has been released as the third Kali update of 2026, bringing six new penetration testing tools, Linux kernel 7.1.5, KDE Plasma 6.7, refreshed image-building scripts, and a large set of Kali NetHunter changes. The release arrived on October 26 with 126 package updates and moves the kernel from version 6.19 to 7.1.5.

The update follows June’s Kali Linux 2026.2 release, which added nine tools, changed Kali’s APT source format, and improved virtual machine boot times. It also continues the tool and mobile testing work seen in Kali Linux 2026.1, the first major Kali update of the year.

## Six New Penetration Testing Tools

The six new tools are available from Kali’s network repositories. Dalfox is an open-source cross-site scripting scanner built for automation and parameter checks.

Katana is a crawling and spidering framework that can help researchers map web applications and find paths, files, and endpoints before deeper testing.

Qsreplace takes URLs from standard input and replaces query string values with a chosen value, which makes it useful for preparing URL lists for repeatable web tests.

Rustscan is a fast port scanner written in Rust. It can scan large port ranges and pass discovered ports to Nmap for deeper service checks. SDRangel is a Qt-based software-defined radio front end that supports devices such as RTL-SDR, BladeRF, and HackRF, giving wireless researchers a visual tool for receiving, sending, and studying radio signals.

Snaffler-ng searches readable Windows SMB shares for credentials and sensitive data. It supports NTLM and Kerberos sign-in, DFS discovery, archive checks, built-in classification rules, SQLite resume support, and several output formats.

These additions cover web discovery, XSS testing, URL processing, port scanning, radio research, and file-share review. Like any security tool, they should only be used on systems that the tester owns or has clear permission to assess.

## Linux Kernel 7.1.5 and Package Updates

Kali 2026.3 contains 126 package updates and moves the main Kali kernel from 6.19 to 7.1.5. Kali’s package tracker lists 7.1.5-1kali1 for the rolling branch, confirming the kernel used by the new release.

The newer kernel matters because it provides the base for hardware support, drivers, system calls, and security fixes used by the rest of the distribution. Users should still test wireless adapters, graphics drivers, virtualization tools, and any custom kernel modules before relying on the update during live security work.

One of the largest changes is the refresh of Kali’s public build scripts. These are the same scripts the project uses to create the official images offered through its download site. The refreshed scripts now have a more consistent structure, layout, command-line options, features, and output across supported platforms.

Each refreshed project includes a build-in-container.sh script. It detects whether Docker or Podman is present, creates a build container, and runs the image build inside that container. This removes the earlier need to build Kali on a Kali system and makes the process easier to repeat on other Debian-based hosts. Kali has also improved its related build documentation.

Users who want to build a standard installer can clone the kali-installer build repository, install the required packages, and run sudo ./build.sh. The default command creates a Kali rolling installer for AMD64. Builders can change the hostname, add packages such as Rustscan, select kali-dev, choose a netinst image, or target ARM64 through command-line options. Podman users can instead install Podman and run sudo ./build-in-container.sh.

The work is not finished. Kali says some build scripts did not make the 2026.3 deadline, and the remaining refresh is planned for Kali 2026.4. Later stages are expected to focus on automated builds, workflows, example setups, and deeper customization. Teams with CI jobs based on the older scripts should review their pipelines because changes made during the refresh may have broken older workflows.

## KDE Plasma 6.7 and New Icons

The optional KDE desktop has been updated to Plasma 6.7. A key feature is per-screen virtual desktops, which lets users change the workspace on one monitor without changing every display.

This can be useful when keeping Burp Suite on one screen, terminals on another, and notes or documentation on a third. Plasma’s Overview also supports faster desktop switching by scrolling or using Page Up and Page Down.

KDE Plasma 6.7 adds more Wayland protocol and portal support, better performance and lower power use for integrated Intel graphics, CPU-rendered applications, and setups with many full-screen windows. Network connections can be duplicated, while System Monitor, software management, printing, background application display, microphone testing, and desktop search controls also receive changes.

KDE has added a light and dark theme switch, improved Breeze, restored the Oxygen and Air styles, and introduced an early preview of its Union theming system.

Kali has also added icons to tools that did not have them and updated older icons so applications are easier to identify in the menu and on the Kali tools website. Xfce remains Kali’s default desktop even though KDE received the main desktop version change in this release.

## Major Kali NetHunter Changes

Kali NetHunter, the project’s Android and wearable security testing platform, receives some of the release’s most unusual changes. The team addressed compatibility problems between modern systemd and udev components and older mobile kernels without requiring large sets of patches.

Wardriving is now supported on the TicWatch Pro 3 series. An updated libnexmonkali library enables internal Wi-Fi monitor mode on the watch, allowing compatible tools inside the Kali chroot, including Aircrack-ng and Kismet, to work with the watch’s wireless hardware. Kali’s TicWatch guide says all Pro 3 GPS, LTE, Ultra GPS, and Ultra LTE variants are supported, though installation requires bootloader, recovery, operating system, root, and NetHunter changes.

WearHunter is a new experimental feature that lets a user control a NetHunter watch from a phone through ADB over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. It can run commands and install applications, with more functions planned. NFC Arsenal now provides NFC access to the Kali chroot and can read, clone, and edit Mifare Classic cards without an external adapter. The release also adds KernelSU support, allowing a generated installer ZIP to be installed through the KernelSU application when used with a patched kernel.

Other NetHunter work includes a fix for TicWatch Pro 3 reboot problems and early support for devices that do not use a ramdisk. Bluetooth Arsenal’s airplane mode has returned. EvilTwin and Wardriving are easier to start, while custom commands now support Nexmon monitor mode and Wifite. Kali also fixed a crash caused by the NetHunter application’s storage request and delivered other bug fixes and speed improvements.

Nine new device kernels were added. They cover Google Pixel on LineageOS 22.2 with Android 15, Huawei P9 on EMUI 8 or LineageOS 16, LG K20 Plus on LineageOS 14.1, Moto G Stylus 5G 2022 on LineageOS 23.2, Nubia Z17 on LineageOS 22.2, POCO X5 5G and Redmi Note 12 5G on crDroid 12, Redmi Note 5 Pro on LineageOS 18.1, Sony Xperia 10 V on LineageOS 23.2, and Ulefone Armor 34+ on Android 16.

The release announcement also highlighted the Wardriver Project, a 2021 Honda Civic Type R shown at the Cars and Cops event in Altus, Oklahoma. The project was used to show how vehicle culture, wireless research, and cybersecurity can meet in a single build.

## Website and Documentation Updates

Kali has applied the category layout and icons introduced in its desktop menu to kali.org/tools. Users who prefer the older short view can still open the Top 100 tools page.

The documentation set gains three new pages. They explain how to extract and squash vendor firmware for mainline Linux, import a pre-made Kali QEMU virtual machine, and use NetHunter EvilTwin.

Nine existing guides were updated, covering Live USB persistence, graphics problems on bare-metal systems, NetHunter on the TicWatch Pro 3, Kali as a UTM guest, the Xfce FAQ, Kali NetHunter, Raspberry Pi full-disk encryption, setting up a Kali mirror, and SSH configuration.

The release cycle also added four European mirrors. Two are in the Netherlands at mirror.hacker.nl and mirror.netone.nl. Portugal gained mirror.randhost.com, while Switzerland gained kalimirror.velden.media. Kali’s mirror system can direct users to a nearby current server, but its documentation warns against adding extra repositories to the Kali source configuration because mixing repositories can break an installation.

Kali also thanked community members who worked on documentation, tool pages, NetHunter, and package maintenance. The long contributor list reflects how much of the mobile kernel, device, documentation, and packaging work comes from outside contributors rather than only the core Kali team.

## Downloading and Upgrading Kali 2026.3

New users can obtain tested installer, live, virtual machine, ARM, cloud, container, and NetHunter images from the official Kali download page. Kali recommends the latest point-release image for most users. Weekly images contain newer packages and can reduce the number of updates needed after installation, but they are automated and do not receive the same quality checks as standard point-release images.

Existing rolling users should first confirm that /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kali.sources points to the official kali-rolling repository with the main, contrib, non-free, and non-free-firmware components. They can then run sudo apt update followed by sudo apt full-upgrade -y. If the system marks a reboot as required, users should restart before checking the result.

The installed release can be checked with grep VERSION /etc/os-release, which should show 2026.3. The active kernel can be checked with uname -r, with the AMD64 release example showing 7.1.5+kali-amd64. The exact kernel string can differ by architecture.

Kali’s update guidance recommends checking for updates every few days or weeks, or sooner when a required tool or security fix is released. It also advises testing all needed tools before a planned security engagement and avoiding updates during active work because a rolling package change can sometimes break a tool at the wrong time

Kali Linux 2026.3 has been released as the third Kali update of 2026, bringing six new penetration testing tools, Linux kernel 7.1.5, KDE Plasma 6.7, refreshed image-building scripts, and a large set of Kali NetHunter changes. The release arrived on October 26 with 126 package updates and moves the kernel from version 6.19 to 7.1.5.

The update follows June’s Kali Linux 2026.2 release, which added nine tools, changed Kali’s APT source format, and improved virtual machine boot times. It also continues the tool and mobile testing work seen in Kali Linux 2026.1, the first major Kali update of the year.

## Six New Penetration Testing Tools

The six new tools are available from Kali’s network repositories. Dalfox is an open-source cross-site scripting scanner built for automation and parameter checks.

Katana is a crawling and spidering framework that can help researchers map web applications and find paths, files, and endpoints before deeper testing.

Qsreplace takes URLs from standard input and replaces query string values with a chosen value, which makes it useful for preparing URL lists for repeatable web tests.

Rustscan is a fast port scanner written in Rust. It can scan large port ranges and pass discovered ports to Nmap for deeper service checks. SDRangel is a Qt-based software-defined radio front end that supports devices such as RTL-SDR, BladeRF, and HackRF, giving wireless researchers a visual tool for receiving, sending, and studying radio signals.

Snaffler-ng searches readable Windows SMB shares for credentials and sensitive data. It supports NTLM and Kerberos sign-in, DFS discovery, archive checks, built-in classification rules, SQLite resume support, and several output formats.

These additions cover web discovery, XSS testing, URL processing, port scanning, radio research, and file-share review. Like any security tool, they should only be used on systems that the tester owns or has clear permission to assess.

## Linux Kernel 7.1.5 and Package Updates

Kali 2026.3 contains 126 package updates and moves the main Kali kernel from 6.19 to 7.1.5. Kali’s package tracker lists 7.1.5-1kali1 for the rolling branch, confirming the kernel used by the new release.

The newer kernel matters because it provides the base for hardware support, drivers, system calls, and security fixes used by the rest of the distribution. Users should still test wireless adapters, graphics drivers, virtualization tools, and any custom kernel modules before relying on the update during live security work.

One of the largest changes is the refresh of Kali’s public build scripts. These are the same scripts the project uses to create the official images offered through its download site. The refreshed scripts now have a more consistent structure, layout, command-line options, features, and output across supported platforms.

Each refreshed project includes a build-in-container.sh script. It detects whether Docker or Podman is present, creates a build container, and runs the image build inside that container. This removes the earlier need to build Kali on a Kali system and makes the process easier to repeat on other Debian-based hosts. Kali has also improved its related build documentation.

Kali Linux 2026.3 has been released as the third Kali update of 2026, bringing six new penetration testing tools, Linux kernel 7.1.5, KDE Plasma 6.7, refreshed image-building scripts, and a large set of Kali NetHunter changes. The release arrived on October 26 with 126 package updates and moves the kernel from version 6.19 to 7.1.5.

The update follows June’s Kali Linux 2026.2 release, which added nine tools, changed Kali’s APT source format, and improved virtual machine boot times. It also continues the tool and mobile testing work seen in Kali Linux 2026.1, the first major Kali update of the year.

## Six New Penetration Testing Tools

The six new tools are available from Kali’s network repositories. Dalfox is an open-source cross-site scripting scanner built for automation and parameter checks.

Katana is a crawling and spidering framework that can help researchers map web applications and find paths, files, and endpoints before deeper testing.

Qsreplace takes URLs from standard input and replaces query string values with a chosen value, which makes it useful for preparing URL lists for repeatable web tests.

Rustscan is a fast port scanner written in Rust. It can scan large port ranges and pass discovered ports to Nmap for deeper service checks. SDRangel is a Qt-based software-defined radio front end that supports devices such as RTL-SDR, BladeRF, and HackRF, giving wireless researchers a visual tool for receiving, sending, and studying radio signals.

Snaffler-ng searches readable Windows SMB shares for credentials and sensitive data. It supports NTLM and Kerberos sign-in, DFS discovery, archive checks, built-in classification rules, SQLite resume support, and several output formats.

These additions cover web discovery, XSS testing, URL processing, port scanning, radio research, and file-share review. Like any security tool, they should only be used on systems that the tester owns or has clear permission to assess.

## Linux Kernel 7.1.5 and Package Updates

Kali 2026.3 contains 126 package updates and moves the main Kali kernel from 6.19 to 7.1.5. Kali’s package tracker lists 7.1.5-1kali1 for the rolling branch, confirming the kernel used by the new release.

The newer kernel matters because it provides the base for hardware support, drivers, system calls, and security fixes used by the rest of the distribution. Users should still test wireless adapters, graphics drivers, virtualization tools, and any custom kernel modules before relying on the update during live security work.

One of the largest changes is the refresh of Kali’s public build scripts. These are the same scripts the project uses to create the official images offered through its download site. The refreshed scripts now have a more consistent structure, layout, command-line options, features, and output across supported platforms.

Each refreshed project includes a build-in-container.sh script. It detects whether Docker or Podman is present, creates a build container, and runs the image build inside that container. This removes the earlier need to build Kali on a Kali system and makes the process easier to repeat on other Debian-based hosts. Kali has also improved its related build documentation.

Users who want to build a standard installer can clone the kali-installer build repository, install the required packages, and run sudo ./build.sh. The default command creates a Kali rolling installer for AMD64. Builders can change the hostname, add packages such as Rustscan, select kali-dev, choose a netinst image, or target ARM64 through command-line options. Podman users can instead install Podman and run sudo ./build-in-container.sh.

The work is not finished. Kali says some build scripts did not make the 2026.3 deadline, and the remaining refresh is planned for Kali 2026.4. Later stages are expected to focus on automated builds, workflows, example setups, and deeper customization. Teams with CI jobs based on the older scripts should review their pipelines because changes made during the refresh may have broken older workflows.

## KDE Plasma 6.7 and New Icons

The optional KDE desktop has been updated to Plasma 6.7. A key feature is per-screen virtual desktops, which lets users change the workspace on one monitor without changing every display.

This can be useful when keeping Burp Suite on one screen, terminals on another, and notes or documentation on a third. Plasma’s Overview also supports faster desktop switching by scrolling or using Page Up and Page Down.

KDE Plasma 6.7 adds more Wayland protocol and portal support, better performance and lower power use for integrated Intel graphics, CPU-rendered applications, and setups with many full-screen windows. Network connections can be duplicated, while System Monitor, software management, printing, background application display, microphone testing, and desktop search controls also receive changes.

KDE has added a light and dark theme switch, improved Breeze, restored the Oxygen and Air styles, and introduced an early preview of its Union theming system.

Kali has also added icons to tools that did not have them and updated older icons so applications are easier to identify in the menu and on the Kali tools website. Xfce remains Kali’s default desktop even though KDE received the main desktop version change in this release.

## Major Kali NetHunter Changes

Kali NetHunter, the project’s Android and wearable security testing platform, receives some of the release’s most unusual changes. The team addressed compatibility problems between modern systemd and udev components and older mobile kernels without requiring large sets of patches.

Wardriving is now supported on the TicWatch Pro 3 series. An updated libnexmonkali library enables internal Wi-Fi monitor mode on the watch, allowing compatible tools inside the Kali chroot, including Aircrack-ng and Kismet, to work with the watch’s wireless hardware. Kali’s TicWatch guide says all Pro 3 GPS, LTE, Ultra GPS, and Ultra LTE variants are supported, though installation requires bootloader, recovery, operating system, root, and NetHunter changes.

It can run commands and install applications, with more functions planned. The release also adds KernelSU support, allowing a generated installer ZIP to be installed through the KernelSU application when used with a patched kernel.

EvilTwin and Wardriving are easier to start, while custom commands now support Nexmon monitor mode and Wifite. Kali also fixed a crash caused by the NetHunter application’s storage request and delivered other bug fixes and speed improvements.

Nine new device kernels were added. They cover Google Pixel on LineageOS 22.2 with Android 15, Huawei P9 on EMUI 8 or LineageOS 16, LG K20 Plus on LineageOS 14.1, Moto G Stylus 5G 2022 on LineageOS 23.2, Nubia Z17 on LineageOS 22.2, POCO X5 5G and Redmi Note 12 5G on crDroid 12, Redmi Note 5 Pro on LineageOS 18.1, Sony Xperia 10 V on LineageOS 23.2, and Ulefone Armor 34+ on Android 16.
