articles.title: Top 10 Best Data Access Governance Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
articles.summary: Ask any enterprise “who can read the M&A folder?” and watch the room go quiet effective access is buried under nested groups, inherited shares, service-account grants, and warehouse roles nobody has reviewed since the migration.
articles.content:
Ask any enterprise “who can read the M&A folder?” and watch the room go quiet effective access is buried under nested groups, inherited shares, service-account grants, and warehouse roles nobody has reviewed since the migration.

Data access governance (DAG) answers that question continuously and then shrinks the answer. It’s also 2026’s quiet AI prerequisite: every copilot deployment inherits your permission sprawl and surfaces it in chat.

We scored ten tools on visibility truth, remediation muscle, and estate fit. Varonis takes 1; Veza and Immuta complete the podium.

• 1 overall: Varonis the effective-access graph plus automated least-privilege remediation at collaboration scale.

• Podium: Varonis (remediation muscle), Veza (identity-to-data authorization graph), Immuta (warehouse-native policy).

• Copilot effect: AI assistants surface every overexposed file to every user who technically has access DAG is the fix, not the chatbot settings.

• Nonhuman identities: service accounts and pipelines now outnumber humans on data grants; govern them first.

## How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation: effective-access computation (nested groups, inheritance, cross-system), activity-informed right-sizing, automated remediation safety, access-review/certification workflows, estate coverage (collaboration, warehouse, SaaS, infrastructure), and pricing structure.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: effective-access truth 30%, remediation automation 25%, estate coverage 20%, review workflows 15%, pricing clarity 10%.

## The 2026 Data Access Governance Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

## 1. Varonis — Best Effective-Access Remediation

Snapshot: Per-user/quote | Permission graph + audit stream + automated fixes | SaaS-delivered

Why it earns 1: Varonis computes what others estimate true effective access across nested groups and inheritance then watches actual usage and acts: automated removal of unused grants, global-access-group elimination, and continuous least-privilege enforcement that has shrunk blast radius at thousands of organizations.

With Copilot-readiness assessments riding the same engine, it’s the category’s remediation benchmark, not just its dashboard.

Pros: Remediation automation that actually executes; activity-informed decisions; deep M365/file-share/SaaS coverage.

Cons: Warehouse/lakehouse depth lighter than policy-native rivals.

Bottom line: Finds the sprawl, then deletes it safely.

## 2. Veza — Best Authorization Graph

Snapshot: Quote | Identity-to-data effective permissions across systems | NHI-strong

Why it earns 2: Veza’s graph answers the cross-system question nobody else frames as crisply: this identity (human or service account) can take these actions on this data, across warehouses, SaaS, infrastructure, and apps Identity-to-data effective permissions across systems local roles translated into one effective-permission model.

For the nonhuman-identity sprawl defining 2026, it’s the clearest lens on who-can-do-what.

Pros: Cross-system authorization truth; NHI governance strength; access reviews on real permissions, not role names.

Cons: Younger remediation muscle than Varonis in collaboration estates.

Bottom line: The permissions graph your IGA tool thinks it has.

## 3. Immuta — Best Warehouse-Native Policy

Snapshot: Quote/tiered | Plain-language ABAC policies | Native Snowflake/Databricks enforcement

Why it earns 3: Immuta turns governance into enforced policy where analytics lives: attribute-based rules written once (“masks PHI except for care-team roles”) compile into native warehouse controls no proxies, no copies with discovery wiring detected sensitive columns straight into enforcement. The lakehouse lane’s policy anchor.

Pros: Policy-as-code clarity; native pushdown enforcement; discovery-to-policy loop.

Cons: Scoped to analytics platforms, not file/collab estates.

Bottom line: Access governance the warehouse itself enforces.

## 4. Microsoft Purview — Best M365-Estate Governance

Snapshot: E5/bundled | Labels, DLP, access reviews, Restricted SharePoint Search era | Copilot-driven urgency

Why it earns 4: Copilot made Microsoft’s own governance stack urgent: Purview labels and DLP, Entra access reviews, SharePoint Advanced Management, and oversharing assessments form the native toolkit for taming M365 permission sprawl before AI amplifies it.

It’s assembly-required several consoles, E5-tier licensing but it’s the estate’s first-party answer.

Pros: Native depth; bundle economics at E5; Copilot-readiness alignment.

Cons: Fragmented toolchain; effective-access truth still favors specialists.

Bottom line: The first-party toolkit Copilot forced onto every roadmap.

## 5. SailPoint — Best IGA-Integrated Data Governance

Snapshot: Quote | Data Access Security (file-access governance) inside the IGA leader

Why it earns 5: SailPoint extends identity governance to unstructured data Data Access Security (file-access governance) inside the IGA leader delivers discovery of overexposure, access reviews, and remediation requests in the same platform that already runs joiner-mover-leaver and certifications.

For enterprises standardized on SailPoint IGA, folding data access into existing governance rhythms beats bolting on a parallel program.

Pros: One governance program for apps and data; certification-campaign maturity.

Cons: Analytics depth trails the data-native specialists.

Bottom line: Data access inside the identity-governance machine.

## 6. BigID — Best Discovery-Anchored Governance

Snapshot: Quote | Access intelligence on the discovery graph | Who-can-access-what-sensitive-data

Why it earns 6: BigID starts from the data truth it already owns classified, correlated inventory and layers access intelligence: which identities can reach which sensitive classes, where open access meets regulated data, and remediation workflows scoped by sensitivity rather than folder names. Governance that knows what the data is first.

Pros: Sensitivity-weighted access risk; one engine for discovery + governance; privacy-use synergy.

Cons: Remediation execution depth behind Varonis.

Bottom line: Access risk ranked by what the data actually is.

## 7. Netwrix — Best Mid-Market Auditing Value

Snapshot: Licensed | Auditor + Data Classification + PolicyPak lineage | AD/file-share strength

Why it earns 7: Netwrix gives mid-market teams the working core who has access, who used it, what changed, with classification context and review workflows across AD, file shares, and M365 at licensing that doesn’t require a platform committee.

Pros: Approachable pricing/operations; strong AD/change context; suite synergy.

Cons: Enterprise-scale graph analytics and automation lighter.

Bottom line: The pragmatic mid-market governance workhorse.

## 8. Privacera — Best Open-Standard Lakehouse Control

Snapshot: Quote | Apache Ranger lineage | Unified policies across cloud data services

Why it earns 8: Built by Ranger’s creators, Privacera applies unified policies across lakehouse and cloud data services attractive for platform teams wanting Ranger-compatible governance without proprietary lock-in, with encryption and masking in the same policy plane.

Pros: Open-source lineage; multi-service policy unification.

Cons: Ecosystem gravity behind Immuta in the lane.

Bottom line: The open-standard path to lakehouse policy.

## 9. Satori — Best Deploy-Light Warehouse Access

Snapshot: Tiered/quote | Proxy-based, agentless | JIT access + dynamic masking in hours

Why it earns 9: Satori’s transparent access layer delivers governance outcomes just-in-time grants, dynamic masking, universal audit over Snowflake-class platforms in hours, no warehouse-side changes. The speed-to-governed pick when the mandate landed last quarter.

Pros: Fastest deployment in the lane; self-service access flows.

Cons: Proxy architecture is a design decision to accept.

Bottom line: Warehouse governance measured in hours, not quarters.

## 4. Microsoft Purview — Best M365-Estate Governance

## Buying Advice: Fix One Folder, Then Trust the Automation

Prove value on the crown jewels first: pick your most sensitive repository, have each finalist compute true effective access (nested groups and service accounts included compare against a manual audit), then let it right-size based on actual usage and measure how many grants die without a single access complaint.

If Copilot or an equivalent assistant is deploying, run an oversharing assessment before enablement AI turns latent overexposure into daily exposure.

What is the best data access governance tool in 2026? Varonis ranks 1 for effective-access truth plus automated remediation, Veza for the cross-system authorization graph, and Immuta for warehouse-native policy with Purview the M365 first-party toolkit and Netwrix the mid-market value pick.

How is DAG different from IGA? IGA governs accounts and app entitlements; DAG governs what identities can actually do to data resolving nested groups, shares, and warehouse roles into effective access, then shrinking it. Mature programs connect both (SailPoint and Veza sit at that junction).

Why did Copilot make DAG urgent? AI assistants retrieve anything the asking user can technically access permission sprawl that hid behind obscurity becomes one prompt away. Oversharing assessment and least-privilege remediation are the prerequisite, not a post-launch fix.

What about service accounts and pipelines? Nonhuman identities now dominate data grants and are never recertified by habit. Demand NHI visibility (Veza-class) and include them in review campaigns from day one.

How do we run access reviews that aren’t rubber stamps? Review effective access with usage evidence attached “can read, hasn’t in 14 months” and default to removal with easy re-grant. Tools that present role names without usage data produce the rubber stamps you’re trying to escape.

Varonis deletes the sprawl, Veza maps it across every system that grants it, Immuta compiles policy into the warehouse itself, and Purview is the first-party kit Copilot made mandatory pilot on your crown-jewel folder, certify the service accounts first, and judge every tool by grants removed without complaints, the category’s only honest metric.

articles.title: U.S. Soldier Gets 70 Months in Prison for AT&T, Verizon Extortions
articles.summary: A U.S. Army soldier who pleaded guilty to hacking into multiple telecommunications companies and stealing mobile call and text metadata for more than 100 million AT&T customers in 2024 was sentenced to 70 months in federal prison today and ordered to
articles.content:
A U.S. Army soldier who pleaded guilty to hacking into multiple telecommunications companies and stealing mobile call and text metadata for more than 100 million AT&T customers in 2024 was sentenced to 70 months in federal prison today and ordered to pay nearly $300,000 in restitution to victims.

One of several selfies from the Facebook page of Cameron Wagenius.

Cameron John Wagenius, 22, was stationed at a U.S. Army base in South Korea when he adopted the cybercriminal persona “Kiberphant0m.” Working with three alleged co-conspirators, Kiberphant0m downloaded data from several large customers of the cloud data storage service Snowflake that had exposed credentials and did not enforce multi-factor authentication (Snowflake has since mandated MFA on all accounts).

In October 2024, Kiberphant0m bragged on the cybercrime forums that he’d stolen the call and text metadata (e.g. source and destination number, timestamp, duration, etc.) for tens of millions of AT&T customers. Kiberphant0m claimed to have hacked into more than dozen telecommunications companies worldwide, including Verizon’s Push-to-Talk business, and publicly extorted these companies in exchange for a promise not to publish the stolen data.

In late November 2025, KrebsOnSecurity warned that Kiberphant0m was likely a U.S. soldier stationed in South Korea. Less than a month later, Wagenius was arrested and charged in two separate federal indictments, and soon pleaded guilty to all counts in both cases.

At his sentencing hearing in Seattle today, Wagenius was sentenced to nearly six years in federal prison, and ordered to pay $294,978 in restitution.

Federal prosecutors said Wagenius was assisted in his efforts to extort victim companies by Kenneth Schuchman, a 28-year old man from Vancouver, Washington who has a lengthy cybercriminal history. In 2019, Schuchman pleaded guilty to operating the Satori botnet, a vast collection of hacked Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices that was used for large-scale distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks.

Two other alleged co-conspirators of Wagenius are still facing charges in connection with the Snowflake data thefts; Conor Riley Moucka, a.k.a. “Judische,” of Kitchener, Ontario was arrested in 2024 and pleaded guilty in August 2026; and John Erin Binns, an American man currently living in Turkey who is also wanted for a 2021 data breach at T-Mobile that exposed the personal information of at least 76 million customers.

Kiberphant0m also admitted to re-extorting victims, and threatening to disclose national security secrets. Immediately following Moucka’s arrest — after AT&T had already paid the extortion group a $370,000 Bitcoin ransom — Kiberphant0m posted on hacker forums what he claimed were the AT&T call logs for then President-elect Donald Trump and for then Vice President Kamala Harris, as well as schematics allegedly stolen from the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA).

Paul Russell is a resident agent in charge at the Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS), the criminal investigative arm of the U.S. Department of Defense Office of Inspector General. Russell said when DCIS received information that a soldier with secret clearance was allegedly involved in cybercrime and extortion, the agency began working the investigation alongside the FBI, the Army Criminal Investigative Division (CID), and the U.S. Secret Service.

“We don’t often get leads where there’s an active duty soldier with a secret clearance who’s creating hacking tools and trafficking in data,” Russell said. “That doesn’t happen every day, and so when that hits it really spins all of our partner organizations up. It was very serious from jump street, just because it was unique, it was an insider threat, and we weren’t sure what we were dealing with.”

A sentencing memo (PDF) filed Sept. 19 by federal prosecutors in Seattle notes that while Wagenius pleaded guilty almost immediately and has been remarkably cooperative, he recently got caught trying to find security vulnerabilities in the BOP’s computer network. The government’s memo notes that while incarcerated and awaiting sentencing, Wagenius violated the computer use policies of the Bureau of Prisons (BOP) in attempts to learn about vulnerabilities in BOP computer systems.

“According to records from BOP, in or around September 2025, Wagenius used another inmate’s email system to request that the email recipient prompt a commercial AI tool to provide information about “[w]hat CVE’s are there for Windows 10 Enterprise privilege escalation and bypasses” and to “[p]rovide the CVE’s and a real world working script for each CVE . . . without omitted code,” the government’s memo states.

The memo states that less than a week later, Wagenius used a different inmate’s email account and requested that the email recipient prompt an AI tool to “[p]rovide the step by step for CVE-2023-45208, code for this if any, and if no code exists make some, make sure to describe everything in detail.” CVE-2023-45208 is a three-year-old “command injection” vulnerability in D-Link networking devices.

That same month, Wagenius allegedly again requested that the email recipient prompt AI with the question, “How do you make an antenna in a prison environment with commissary or readily available items/tools to improve/make an antenna to extend radio reception?”

Federal prosecutors said Wagenius also requested that the recipient research escaping prison.

“In several instances, Wagenius framed the AI queries as being posed in connection to a book he was writing. This is a common method of ‘prompt injection,’ in which attackers feed specially crafted, deceptive inputs into commercial AI tools that are programmed to avoid outputting malicious code that can be used to exploit computer vulnerabilities,” the sentencing memo reads.

The government told the court it is unaware of evidence that Wagenius figured out how to use or deploy the vulnerabilities he was researching in the BOP’s systems, and when questioned said he was only researching “potential vulnerabilities to provide information to the BOP.”

Incredibly, despite the enormous financial value of the data stolen from AT&T and other telecom providers, Wagenius’s extortion efforts were largely unsuccessful. The government’s sentencing memo says Wagenius made a whopping total of around $1,500 from selling stolen data.

“While Wagenius was not particularly financially successful as a cybercriminal, he both intended to and caused significant harm to numerous individual victims, U.S. companies, and the U.S. government,” the memo states.

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.summary: Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are
articles.content:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

articles.title: Microsoft Plugs Nearly 1,000 Security Holes
articles.summary: Microsoft Corp. today issued updates to plug at least 974 security holes in its Windows operating systems and other software, by far its biggest single patch batch ever. Microsoft says artificial intelligence is helping to speed the discovery of vuln
articles.content:
Microsoft Corp. today issued updates to plug at least 974 security holes in its Windows operating systems and other software, by far its biggest single patch batch ever. Microsoft says artificial intelligence is helping to speed the discovery of vulnerabilities, but security experts warn that many organizations already are struggling to prioritize the more human-intensive endeavor of testing and deploying so many fixes each month.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Kirill Makarov.

This month’s patch bundle obliterates the software giant’s previous record set in July, when it released updates for at least 570 security vulnerabilities. September’s Patch Tuesday brings this year’s total to more than 2,600, more than twice Microsoft’s previous record-setting patch year in 2020 (1,245) and with three more months to go.

There are two “zero-day” flaws fixed this month that are being actively exploited: both CVE-2026-81963 and CVE-2026-85880 allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on Windows system.

Fully 113 of the bugs addressed today earned Microsoft’s “critical” rating, meaning they could be abused by malware or miscreants to seize control over a vulnerable Windows machine with little or no help from the user.

Among the more serious critical flaws this month is CVE-2026-69730, a DNS weakness present in Windows Server 2012 onward and on Windows 10. Microsoft warns that an unauthenticated attacker could leverage this weakness simply by sending a specially crafted packet to an affected system, and that it is likely to be exploited.

Also scary is CVE-2026-69829, a critical, remote code execution flaw in the Windows Shell. This vulnerability has a CVSS base score of 9.8 (10 is the most severe), and can be exploited with low attack complexity, no privileges, and no user interaction.

Microsoft’s summary of the security updates released today. Image: msrc.microsoft.com.

Microsoft is hardly alone in shipping monster patch bundles lately. Many other large software companies, including Adobe, Cisco, Google, Mozilla and Oracle, all have recently credited AI-assisted research with increasing their patch cadence and volume (Google said today it is now going to ship security updates every two weeks).

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, said one core challenge with deploying Windows updates is that they need to be tested before being installed across an organization because not all third-party software works seamlessly in the face of changes to the underlying operating system.

“It’s time to put our CISOs and CSOs on notice,” Reguly said. “How are you helping your teams through these difficult times? Do you have your teams deploy after hours and on weekends to avoid disruption to the business environment? Do you reward them for that effort? Time to dig into your budget and buy dinner for your teams that are working on Saturday to get patches rolled out before users return to work on Monday.”

Satnam Narang is senior staff research engineer at Tenable. Narang said it’s important to recognize that while the number of vulnerabilities being patched by Microsoft is rising, the number of flaws that can and will affect most organizations remains quite low.

“AI-assisted vulnerability discovery in 2026 is creating larger haystacks, but it isn’t finding more needles,” he said. “It’s critical that organizations understand which vulnerabilities actually apply to them, whether they pose a threat by being reachable and exploitable, and prioritize remediation based on this risk context.”

Of course, regular Windows users don’t need to test patches before deploying them, but they still need to open Windows Update periodically or else assent to the program’s nag notices about pending updates. And at the rate these Windows patch releases are ballooning in size, it’s probably best not to let them pile up month after month.

Enterprise Windows admins will want to keep an eye on askwoody.com for news of any updates that appear to be causing problems. As always, the SANS Internet Storm Center has a per-patch breakdown ordered by severity and urgency.

articles.title: SBI Notifies Customers Impacted by the Recent Cyber Incident
articles.summary: State Bank of India (SBI) has individually notified customers whose information was identified in a recent cyber incident, sending alerts through email and WhatsApp.
articles.content:
State Bank of India (SBI) has individually notified customers whose information was identified in a recent cyber incident, sending alerts through email and WhatsApp.

In its latest advisory on October 23, the bank said customer account balances and funds remain safe while investigators examine the suspected exposure of personal information found on the dark web.

The update shifts the bank’s response from an initial public disclosure to direct communication with customers. According to The Economic Times, SBI said it had informed all customers whose data was identified as involved.

The bank also warned users to stay alert for suspicious calls, messages, and emails, and never share passwords, PINs, or one-time passwords.

SBI’s preliminary review examined approximately 375,000 records available on the dark web and identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information.

These figures represent different measures. The larger number describes the records reviewed, not a confirmed count of affected SBI customers or compromised bank accounts.

## SBI Notifies Customers Impacted By Cyber Incident

The information reportedly included names, registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses and home addresses. Other fields included gender, branch details, Customer Information File identifiers, and information linked to loan inquiries and lead records. These details can identify customers and provide context about their banking relationships.

As covered in Cybersecurity News’ earlier report on the SBI data loss incident, the disclosure did not establish how the information was obtained.

It also did not confirm that attackers had entered SBI’s core banking systems. No publicly identified entry point, exploited software flaw, or malware family explained the incident.

SBI received alerts on October 16 from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defense Cyber Agency, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, known as CERT-In.

The bank activated its incident response and containment procedures and appointed an independent cybersecurity agency impaneled with CERT-In to investigate.

Investigators are examining the authenticity, source and extent of the exposed information. SBI has said the incident caused no material impact on its core operations, financial performance or business continuity. Banking services continued without disruption, according to the bank’s disclosure.

An earlier unverified claim about an SBI data breach alleged that customer records and banking documents had been posted online. Those allegations should remain separate from SBI’s confirmed findings while the investigation continues.

Personal data exposure does not automatically mean an account has been taken over. Available reporting does not establish that passwords, PINs, OTPs, or transaction credentials were compromised. However, exposed contact and loan details could help criminals create convincing messages that appear to come from the bank.

Customers should verify unexpected notifications through official banking channels rather than trust a message because it contains accurate personal details. They should avoid unfamiliar links and check statements for unauthorized transactions.

SBI’s official cybersecurity guidance lists report.phishing@sbi.co.in for reporting cyber incidents and directs users to India’s cybercrime helpline, 1930. The bank’s latest warning stresses that customers must never disclose authentication codes or banking passwords to anyone.

The post SBI Notifies Customers Impacted by the Recent Cyber Incident appeared first on Cyber Security News.

The 2026 winners solve for both ends sender-side automation (policies, DLP triggers, one-click protect) and recipient experiences that don’t require a manual.

We scored ten services on exactly that trade, plus control depth (expiry, revoke, audit) and compliance evidence.

Virtru takes 1; Microsoft Purview and Proofpoint complete the podium.

• 1 overall: Virtru the lowest-friction path to encrypted mail recipients actually open.

• Podium: Virtru (recipient experience), Purview Message Encryption (M365 gravity), Proofpoint (gateway-policy muscle).

• Consolidation flag: Zix, the compliance-encryption veteran, now lives inside OpenText renewal diligence applies.

• Healthcare lane: Paubox’s no-portal delivery is the HIPAA-workflow standout.

## How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation: recipient friction (no-portal/no-account paths), policy automation (DLP-triggered, content-aware encryption), sender controls (expiry, revoke, disable-forward, audit), compliance evidence (HIPAA/GDPR-class), platform fit, and pricing structure.

No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: recipient friction 30%, policy automation 25%, sender controls 20%, compliance evidence 15%, pricing clarity 10%.

## The 2026 Email Encryption Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

## 1. Virtru — Best Recipient Experience

Snapshot: Published tiers | Gmail/Outlook-native | TDF open standard | Expiry, revoke, watermark

Why it earns 1: Virtru wins where encryption actually fails the recipient: external parties open protected messages in a browser without accounts, plugins, or password ping-pong, while senders get one-click protection plus expiry, revocation, disable-forward, and DLP-triggered automation.

Built on the open Trusted Data Format rather than a proprietary silo, it deploys in days on Gmail or M365 and users keep using it, which is the entire game.

Pros: Lowest recipient friction in the lane; strong sender controls; fast deployment; open standard.

Cons: Gateway-class policy breadth is not the aim.

Bottom line: Encryption people don’t route around.

## 2. Microsoft Purview Message Encryption — Best M365-Native

Snapshot: E3/E5-bundled | Label and rule-driven | Office-native reading experience

Why it earns 2: For M365 estates, Purview Message Encryption is capability already licensed: encryption triggered by sensitivity labels and transport rules, seamless reading inside the Microsoft world, and a tolerable one-time-passcode path outside it.

Configure this floor before paying anyone then buy only for the friction and control gaps you can still name.

Pros: Bundle economics; label-driven automation; in-ecosystem seamlessness.

Cons: External-recipient OTP flow is serviceable, not delightful; advanced controls fragment across SKUs.

Bottom line: The floor every M365 tenant should fully enable.

## 3. Proofpoint — Best Gateway-Policy Encryption

Snapshot: Quote/tiered | Encryption inside the leading SEG | Content-aware triggers

Why it earns 3: Proofpoint encrypts as a function of the gateway that already reads every outbound message: DLP dictionaries, smart identifiers, and policy routes trigger encryption automatically no user decisions required with enterprise reporting attached.

For organizations that want encryption as enforced policy rather than user choice, this leading SEG is the lane’s anchor.

Pros: Policy automation depth; DLP integration; enterprise reporting.

Cons: Portal-based recipient experience; platform cost.

Bottom line: Encryption as outbound policy, enforced by the gateway.

## 4. Paubox — Best No-Portal HIPAA Delivery

Snapshot: Published tiers | TLS-delivered, portal-free | HIPAA-focused, BAA included

Why it earns 4: Paubox’s bet: encrypted email should land in the recipient’s normal inbox, readable like any message no portal, no passcode with secure fallback only when TLS can’t be verified.

For healthcare workflows where patients and partners won’t tolerate portals, that design plus HIPAA-focused, BAA included protections made it the clinic-to-enterprise favorite.

Pros: Zero recipient friction; HIPAA-purposed with BAA; honest fallback design.

Cons: Sender-side controls (revoke/expiry) lighter than rights-based rivals.

Bottom line: HIPAA email that reads like email.

## 5. Mimecast — Best Suite-Integrated Secure Messaging

Snapshot: Tiered | Secure Messaging inside the email-security suite | Policy-driven

Why it earns 5: Mimecast folds Secure Messaging inside the email-security suite already handling hygiene, continuity, and archiving one admin plane, policy-triggered protection, and a portal flow recipients see across thousands of Mimecast-protected brands. Consolidation value for its large installed base.

Pros: Suite consolidation; policy automation; familiar at scale.

Cons: Portal experience; deepest value only inside the suite.

Bottom line: The suite shop’s encryption checkbox, competently done.

Snapshot: Licensed | ESA/CES-integrated encryption service | Enterprise policy ties

Why it earns 6: Cisco’s encryption service rides its email-security estate with an ESA/CES-integrated encryption service, registered-envelope delivery, policy triggers, and the procurement comfort of the networking incumbent a rational pick where Cisco already owns the mail path.

Pros: Cisco-estate integration; enterprise procurement fit.

Cons: Envelope/portal recipient flow; innovation pace.

Bottom line: The Cisco estate’s native encryption lane.

## 7. Echoworx — Best Encryption-Delivery Specialist

Snapshot: Quote | Encryption-only focus | Multiple delivery methods per recipient

Why it earns 7: Echoworx does one thing with unusual care: delivery-method intelligence that picks the best path per recipient TLS, portal, attachment, certificate with strong branding control and multi-language support, which is why banks and insurers white-label it.

Pros: Delivery-method flexibility; white-label depth; specialist focus.

Cons: Point solution in a suite-consolidating market.

Bottom line: The delivery-intelligence specialist behind big brands.

## 8. OpenText (Zix) — Best Compliance-Lineage Encryption

Snapshot: Tiered | Zix heritage | Transparent Zix-to-Zix community delivery

Why it earns 8: Zix built the healthcare/finance compliance-encryption franchise including its signature transparent delivery between Zix-community members and now operates inside OpenText’s portfolio.

The installed base is vast; buyers should confirm roadmap investment and packaging under OpenText at renewal.

Pros: Compliance pedigree; community transparent delivery; large regulated base.

Cons: Portfolio-era roadmap diligence.

Bottom line: The compliance veteran, now under a bigger roof.

## 9. Trend Micro — Best Bundled Email-Security Encryption

Snapshot: Bundled/tiered | Encryption within email security | Hosted key service

Why it earns 9: Trend delivers policy-triggered encryption as part of its email-security bundle a pragmatic checkbox for estates already standardized on Trend’s stack rather than a destination purchase.

Pros: Bundle convenience; policy triggers.

Cons: Not the lane’s innovation driver.

Bottom line: Fine where Trend already guards the mail.

## 10. Barracuda — Best SMB-Bundle Encryption

Snapshot: Published bundles | Encryption inside Email Protection plans | SMB-friendly

Why it earns 10: Barracuda includes encryption in SMB-priced email-protection bundles simple policies, simple portal, one invoice the honest answer for small teams who need the checkbox met without an encryption project.

Pros: SMB pricing and simplicity.

Cons: Control depth and recipient polish are basic.

Bottom line: The small-business checkbox, affordably ticked.

## Full Comparison Table

## Yes/No Capability Table

## Buying Advice: Send One Message to Your Hardest Recipient

Run the only test that predicts adoption: send an encrypted message to a real external recipient the 70-year-old patient, the counterparty on Gmail, the vendor on Exchange 2016 and count their clicks to reading it.

More than two, and your users will eventually bypass the tool. Configure your bundle floor first (Purview or Workspace rules), then buy for named gaps: recipient friction (Virtru/Paubox-class), gateway-grade policy enforcement (Proofpoint-class), or white-label delivery (Echoworx-class).

Make encryption automatic DLP and label triggers, never user memory because the breach email is always the one someone forgot to protect.

Healthcare: insist on the BAA and test the patient-reply path, not just outbound. And at Zix renewals, price the OpenText-era roadmap against the switching cost honestly.

What is the best email encryption service in 2026? Virtru ranks 1 for recipient experience plus sender controls, Microsoft Purview for M365-bundled automation, and Proofpoint for gateway-enforced policy with Paubox the HIPAA no-portal standout.

Is TLS enough for email encryption? Opportunistic TLS protects most hops but fails silently and proves nothing per-message. Compliance-grade programs need enforced encryption with fallback and evidence which is precisely what this category sells.

Do recipients need accounts to read encrypted mail? Not with the leaders: Virtru reads in-browser, Paubox lands inbox-native, Zix is transparent in-community. Portal-and-password flows are the adoption tax to minimize.

What makes email encryption HIPAA-compliant? A BAA with the vendor, enforced encryption policies, audit trails, and workflow fit so staff actually use it. The tool is necessary; the program makes it compliant.

Can I revoke an email after sending? With rights-based services (Virtru-class, Purview in-ecosystem), yes access checks happen at open, so you can kill it after delivery. Gateway/portal models vary; test it before relying on it.

Virtru proved usable encryption wins, Purview made the floor nearly free for M365 shops, Proofpoint enforces protection nobody has to remember, and Paubox made HIPAA mail read like mail pick by your hardest recipient’s click count, automate the trigger, and let the bundle-vs-gap math decide the invoice.

articles.title: Fortinet Urges Customers to Patch Critical Flaws Affecting FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer
articles.summary: Fortinet has urged customers to prioritize security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer scheduled for October 22, 2026. The coordinated release addresses critical and high-severity vulnerabilities, including flaws found through AI-as
articles.content:
Fortinet has urged customers to prioritize security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer scheduled for October 22, 2026. The coordinated release addresses critical and high-severity vulnerabilities, including flaws found through AI-assisted security testing. The company said customers should address internet-facing devices first.

In an October 21 announcement, Fortinet Chief Information Security Officer Carl Windsor warned customers against treating these fixes as routine maintenance. The update follows security releases for FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator, extending the patching effort across several key products.

Fortinet said its testing program uses advanced AI models to examine code paths, protocol handling, and configuration logic. The company thanked Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and SpaceX for their work with its security teams.

The concern extends beyond finding new bugs. Fortinet warned that attackers can use AI to compare patched and older software, identify changed code, and build exploits within hours or days. This process, known as patch diffing, can expose weaknesses before customers finish upgrading.

AI may also help attackers combine lower-severity flaws into a more serious attack chain. However, the announcement does not provide individual CVE identifiers, CVSS scores, or detailed attack conditions for this release. It also does not report active exploitation of these newly addressed flaws.

Its earlier testing report also stressed human review. Security analysts validate AI findings and test whether they are exploitable, helping separate real vulnerabilities from false alarms and recommend product security improvements.

## Affected Versions and Required Updates

FortiOS customers should move to version 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13, or 7.2.14, depending on their current branch. Affected releases span 8.0.0–8.0.1, 7.6.0–7.6.7, 7.4.0–7.4.12, and 7.2.0–7.2.13.

FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer share the same minimum fixed releases: 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12, and 7.2.13. Their affected versions cover 8.0.0–8.0.1, 7.6.0–7.6.7, 7.4.0–7.4.11, and 7.2.0–7.2.12. Fortinet lists October 22 availability for all these updates.

For FortiMail, the fixed versions are 8.0.2, 7.6.7, and 7.4.9. Customers running affected FortiMail 7.2 releases must move to the 7.4 branch or later. FortiAuthenticator users should install 8.0.4 or 6.6.11, depending on their branch.

Fortinet plans to publish public advisories on its PSIRT page on November 10. Its notice says FortiSASE will receive automatic updates before the coordinated release. FortiManager Cloud updates may require manual action, while public cloud updates follow the relevant cloud provider’s release process.

The gap between firmware availability and full public disclosure gives customers time to upgrade before detailed advisories appear. It does not mean exposed devices can safely wait until November. Fortinet explicitly asks customers to act when the updates become available, rather than delay for technical details.

## PHP and Node.js Add Patching Pressure

The warning comes alongside separate PHP and Node.js security releases. These are distinct issues, not confirmed components of the Fortinet vulnerabilities.

PHP released emergency patches on October 21 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, known as PHP2Shell. Both can allow remote code execution without authentication. One involves memory exhaustion leaving incomplete request data, while the other involves stale request state surviving after memory is freed.

Cybersecurity News’s PHP2Shell coverage explains the risks across different server setups. Fixed PHP releases are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The PHP Foundation also described how AI-assisted research contributed to investigating these weaknesses.

Separately, the Node.js security update addresses ten vulnerabilities, including four rated high severity. CVE-2026-111497 affects Brotli decompression and can allow code execution through an out-of-bounds memory write. Other high-severity fixes address TLS hostname verification bypasses and DNS name truncation. The affected supported branches are 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

Fortinet recommends identifying exposed systems, backing up configurations, and scheduling urgent maintenance windows for October 22–23. Teams should review logs for unusual administrator access and unauthorized configuration changes before and after patching.

Where upgrades cannot happen immediately, administrators should restrict HTTPS and SSH management to trusted addresses, remove FortiManager administration from the public internet, and enforce multifactor authentication with unique passwords. These controls reduce exposure but do not replace installing the security updates.

es.title: Fortinet Urges Customers to Patch Critical Flaws Affecting FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer
es.summary: Fortinet has urged customers to prioritize security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer scheduled for October 22, 2026. The coordinated release addresses critical and high-severity vulnerabilities, including flaws found through AI-as
es.content:
Fortinet has urged customers to prioritize security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer scheduled for October 22, 2026. The coordinated release addresses critical and high-severity vulnerabilities, including flaws found through AI-assisted security testing. The company said customers should address internet-facing devices first.

In an October 21 announcement, Fortinet Chief Information Security Officer Carl Windsor warned customers against treating these fixes as routine maintenance. The update follows security releases for FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator, extending the patching effort across several key products.

Fortinet said its testing program uses advanced AI models to examine code paths, protocol handling, and configuration logic. The company thanked Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and SpaceX for their work with its security teams.

The concern extends beyond finding new bugs. Fortinet warned that attackers can use AI to compare patched and older software, identify changed code, and build exploits within hours or days. This process, known as patch diffing, can expose weaknesses before customers finish upgrading.

AI may also help attackers combine lower-severity flaws into a more serious attack chain. However, the announcement does not provide individual CVE identifiers, CVSS scores, or detailed attack conditions for this release. It also does not report active exploitation of these newly addressed flaws.

Its earlier testing report also stressed human review. Security analysts validate AI findings and test whether they are exploitable, helping separate real vulnerabilities from false alarms and recommend product security improvements.

## Affected Versions and Required Updates

FortiOS customers should move to version 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13, or 7.2.14, depending on their current branch. Affected releases span 8.0.0–8.0.1, 7.6.0–7.6.7, 7.4.0–7.4.12, and 7.2.0–7.2.13.

FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer share the same minimum fixed releases: 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12, and 7.2.13. Their affected versions cover 8.0.0–8.0.1, 7.6.0–7.6.7, 7.4.0–7.4.11, and 7.2.0–7.2.12. Fortinet lists October 22 availability for all these updates.

For FortiMail, the fixed versions are 8.0.2, 7.6.7, and 7.4.9. Customers running affected FortiMail 7.2 releases must move to the 7.4 branch or later. FortiAuthenticator users should install 8.0.4 or 6.6.11, depending on their branch.

Fortinet plans to publish public advisories on its PSIRT page on November 10. Its notice says FortiSASE will receive automatic updates before the coordinated release. FortiManager Cloud updates may require manual action, while public cloud updates follow the relevant cloud provider’s release process.

The gap between firmware availability and full public disclosure gives customers time to upgrade before detailed advisories appear. It does not mean exposed devices can safely wait until November. Fortinet explicitly asks customers to act when the updates become available, rather than delay for technical details.

## PHP and Node.js Add Patching Pressure

The warning comes alongside separate PHP and Node.js security releases. These are distinct issues, not confirmed components of the Fortinet vulnerabilities.

PHP released emergency patches on October 21 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, known as PHP2Shell. Both can allow remote code execution without authentication. One involves memory exhaustion leaving incomplete request data, while the other involves stale request state surviving after memory is freed.

Cybersecurity News’s PHP2Shell coverage explains the risks across different server setups. Fixed PHP releases are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The PHP Foundation also described how AI-assisted research contributed to investigating these weaknesses.

Separately, the Node.js security update addresses ten vulnerabilities, including four rated high severity. CVE-2026-111497 affects Brotli decompression and can allow code execution through an out-of-bounds memory write. Other high-severity fixes address TLS hostname verification bypasses and DNS name truncation. The affected supported branches are 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

Fortinet recommends identifying exposed systems, backing up configurations, and scheduling urgent maintenance windows for October 22–23. Teams should review logs for unusual administrator access and unauthorized configuration changes before and after patching.

Where upgrades cannot happen immediately, administrators should restrict HTTPS and SSH management to trusted addresses, remove FortiManager administration from the public internet, and enforce multifactor authentication with unique passwords. These controls reduce exposure but do not replace installing the security updates.

articles.title: Samsung and Vizio Smart TVs Still Send Tracking-Like Traffic After Users Turn It Off
articles.summary: Samsung and Vizio smart TVs kept sending traffic consistent with automatic content recognition (ACR) even after researchers turned off the feature in the privacy settings.
articles.content:
Samsung and Vizio smart TVs kept sending traffic consistent with automatic content recognition (ACR) even after researchers turned off the feature in the privacy settings.

The findings raise questions about whether smart TV privacy controls stop viewing-related data flows, while also clarifying an important limit. Encrypted traffic prevented researchers from confirming exactly what these devices transmitted.

The Watching the Watchers study examined 12 commercial televisions from ten manufacturers across eight operating systems representing roughly 95% of the U.S. smart TV market.

Researchers ran 5,943 automated experiments, comparing network activity with automatic content recognition enabled and disabled.

## Samsung TV Tracking After Users Turn It Off

ACR identifies screen content using short audio or video samples, or digital fingerprints derived from them. Providers compare these signals against known content to identify programs. Viewing records can support audience measurement, targeted advertising, and data sharing.

## Samsung, Vizio TVs Continue Tracking After Opt-Out

The feature can monitor content beyond streaming apps, including antenna broadcasts and HDMI devices. Earlier Cyber Security News coverage of smart TV tracking described how ACR can operate even when a television serves mainly as an external display.

For the new analysis, researchers captured network packets. At the same time, televisions played controlled content through antenna inputs, HDMI connections, streaming services, and screen mirroring. Each viewing scenario was repeated with ACR enabled and after opting out.

Samsung’s Tizen television showed ACR-consistent traffic in all 30 opted-out tests involving its built-in streaming service. Similar traffic appeared in 41 of 60 antenna tests, 18 of 30 HDMI tests, and six of 30 Tubi tests.

Vizio’s SmartCast television continued contacting its identified Amazon Kinesis ACR endpoint in every opted-out run for the affected scenarios. Researchers observed no decrease when the feature was disabled.

These findings do not prove that Samsung or Vizio continued recording viewing histories. Most ACR traffic was encrypted, so researchers relied on destinations, timing, volume, and other network patterns. They could not determine what information reached company servers or whether companies stored it.

Opt-outs worked in the tested LG webOS, Sony Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and VIDAA systems. Roku’s setting did not cover its own streaming service, a restriction disclosed on the tested TCL television but not the Roku-branded model.

The research paper also describes risks beyond uncertain encrypted traffic. VIDAA transmitted ACR messages over MQTT without encryption, exposing device identifiers, app names, input sources, and audio fingerprints.

An unauthenticated server exposed more than 57 million detection results linked to over one million televisions. VIDAA subsequently added login requirements, according to the researchers, but transmissions remained unencrypted.

Separately, Vizio’s WatchFree+ service placed readable program or channel information in network names visible through DNS requests and TLS server-name information. This could reveal viewing choices to network observers even with ACR disabled.

Researchers recommend disconnecting the television from the internet or blocking identified ACR endpoints. Their published blocklist did not disrupt viewing in tested scenarios, but it does not stop the WatchFree+ title leak.

Smart TV risks also extend beyond ACR. Separate research into proxy-enabled television apps highlights why app permissions and bundled services deserve scrutiny. These findings apply to the tested devices and firmware, not every television from these brands.

tr.summary: Samsung and Vizio smart TVs kept sending traffic consistent with automatic content recognition (ACR) even after researchers turned off the feature in the privacy settings.
tr.content:
Samsung and Vizio smart TVs kept sending traffic consistent with automatic content recognition (ACR) even after researchers turned off the feature in the privacy settings.

The findings raise questions about whether smart TV privacy controls stop viewing-related data flows, while also clarifying an important limit. Encrypted traffic prevented researchers from confirming exactly what these devices transmitted.

The Watching the Watchers study examined 12 commercial televisions from ten manufacturers across eight operating systems representing roughly 95% of the U.S. smart TV market.

Researchers ran 5,943 automated experiments, comparing network activity with automatic content recognition enabled and disabled.

## Samsung TV Tracking After Users Turn It Off

ACR identifies screen content using short audio or video samples, or digital fingerprints derived from them. Providers compare these signals against known content to identify programs. Viewing records can support audience measurement, targeted advertising, and data sharing.

## Samsung, Vizio TVs Continue Tracking After Opt-Out

The feature can monitor content beyond streaming apps, including antenna broadcasts and HDMI devices. Earlier Cyber Security News coverage of smart TV tracking described how ACR can operate even when a television serves mainly as an external display.

For the new analysis, researchers captured network packets. At the same time, televisions played controlled content through antenna inputs, HDMI connections, streaming services, and screen mirroring. Each viewing scenario was repeated with ACR enabled and after opting out.

Samsung’s Tizen television showed ACR-consistent traffic in all 30 opted-out tests involving its built-in streaming service. Similar traffic appeared in 41 of 60 antenna tests, 18 of 30 HDMI tests, and six of 30 Tubi tests.

Vizio’s SmartCast television continued contacting its identified Amazon Kinesis ACR endpoint in every opted-out run for the affected scenarios. Researchers observed no decrease when the feature was disabled.

These findings do not prove that Samsung or Vizio continued recording viewing histories. Most ACR traffic was encrypted, so researchers relied on destinations, timing, volume, and other network patterns. They could not determine what information reached company servers or whether companies stored it.

Opt-outs worked in the tested LG webOS, Sony Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and VIDAA systems. Roku’s setting did not cover its own streaming service, a restriction disclosed on the tested TCL television but not the Roku-branded model.

The research paper also describes risks beyond uncertain encrypted traffic. VIDAA transmitted ACR messages over MQTT without encryption, exposing device identifiers, app names, input sources, and audio fingerprints.

An unauthenticated server exposed more than 57 million detection results linked to over one million televisions. VIDAA subsequently added login requirements, according to the researchers, but transmissions remained unencrypted.

Separately, Vizio’s WatchFree+ service placed readable program or channel information in network names visible through DNS requests and TLS server-name information. This could reveal viewing choices to network observers even with ACR disabled.

Researchers recommend disconnecting the television from the internet or blocking identified ACR endpoints. Their published blocklist did not disrupt viewing in tested scenarios, but it does not stop the WatchFree+ title leak.

Smart TV risks also extend beyond ACR. Separate research into proxy-enabled television apps highlights why app permissions and bundled services deserve scrutiny. These findings apply to the tested devices and firmware, not every television from these brands.

articles.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
articles.summary: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extor
articles.content:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

## CONFLICTING INTERESTS

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

fr.content:
